OWN QUESTION (C081) — answered in full from the text. Todd's second experiment used buffered lidocaine with epinephrine intradermally at the strengths recorded in the paper card and in the C081 reason (page 724); at the calf, which Table 1 labels 'Leg', mean effective anaesthesia was 1.2 +/- 0.1 h plain against 9.9 +/- 0.9 h with epinephrine, and mean any anaesthesia 2.0 +/- 0.2 h against 11.3 +/- 0.8 h. Those two concentrations appear only in the paper card and in the C081 claim-update reason, per the brief's exception; everywhere else, and for the per-site volume (which the question did not ask about), they are written as [dose figure omitted].

WHAT THE FULL TEXT SETTLED ON DESIGN. Sites compared: forehead near the scalp, volar forearm just distal to the antecubital fossa, dorsum of the non-dominant hand, and medial leg just below the knee (the abstract's 'calf'). Agent: lidocaine, buffered with sodium bicarbonate. Not every site was tested both ways in every subject: all 20 subjects had plain lidocaine at all four sites, and only ten of them returned on a different day for the epinephrine solution at the same four sites, so the paired plain-versus-epinephrine comparison rests on n = 10. Route: an intradermal wheal raised through intact skin on a tuberculin syringe — an intradermal weal, not subcutaneous infiltration. Endpoints: self-marked 21-point pinprick pain-analysis scale, 0 (no painful sensation) to 20 (anaesthetic effect completely absent); duration of EFFECTIVE anaesthesia = time to a score above 5, duration of ANY anaesthesia = time to a score above 19, i.e. essentially complete return of sensation. Assessments every 15 min for plain lidocaine and every 30 min with epinephrine, continued until no effect remained; onset was therefore never timed. Design: unblinded, unrandomised within-subject volunteer experiment, repeated-measures ANOVA with Scheffe post hoc between sites, paired two-tailed t-test for plain versus epinephrine, mean ratios with 95% CIs. No placebo or saline arm. n = 20 healthy ED personnel aged 27-48 (mean 32.0).

THE BODY-LOCALE HALF. Table 1 means in hours (effective, any): face 0.7/1.6 and 3.0/4.2; hand 1.4/2.5 and 6.8/8.1; arm 1.2/2.5 and 8.7/9.3; leg 1.2/2.0 and 9.9/11.3. Only the face differed significantly from the other sites; the sole other significant difference anywhere was hand versus leg with epinephrine. Arm versus leg was not significant by either index, and for plain lidocaine arm versus face did not reach significance either (P = .07). Table 2 ratios to the face for plain lidocaine were 2.1 (arm) and 2.2 (leg) for effective anaesthesia and 1.9 for both on any anaesthesia. Table 3 epinephrine-to-plain ratios were 8.9 (arm) and 8.5 (leg) effective, 4.8 and 4.3 any. So for the same solution the forearm-to-leg step changes duration very little, and the leg was if anything the longest site: reading forearm data across to leg skin is supported for the site variable in healthy skin, which is the step several pages in this record take. One caution for whoever uses this: the paper's headline '1.3- to 13.0-fold' range spans body locales, and its 1.3 lower bound comes from the face on complete recovery, not from the leg.

REFERENCE LIST WORK. All 12 references were worked. The find of the step is reference 5, Christoph 1988 (PMID 2827545): Todd cites it only for its buffering method, but one of its three arms was intradermal lidocaine with epinephrine at the same two strengths as Todd's, in a randomised, prospective, double-blind study of 25 adult volunteers, with onset, extent and duration of skin anaesthesia all recorded. It independently refutes C081 and covers the onset element Todd misses. This record already cites Christoph 1988 at D025 (mepivacaine arm) and D012 (pH comparison) without noticing that arm. References 1 and 4 (Wightman & Vaughn 1976, PMID 791022; Swerdlow & Jones 1970, PMID 4913413) are the primary papers of S-686-39 and S-686-31 in this same job, so they are recorded but not re-judged, to avoid colliding with those workers. Reference 2 (Gramling 1964, PMID 14107177) was looked up as a possible origin of an old mepivacaine duration figure for D025 and set aside: no abstract, no DOI, and MeSH pointing to conduction rather than skin anaesthesia. Reference 10 (Stevenson 1975, JACEP 4:532-535) could not be resolved — two Europe PMC title searches returned hitCount 0 — so its PMID is left blank rather than guessed.

PROBLEMS AND CAVEATS. (a) The extracted text is two-column and the extraction interleaves the columns line by line, so a sentence from pages 724-726 is not contiguous in texts/S-686-35.txt. Following the convention the other workers in this job used, quotes from those pages are joined with ' … ' at each OCR line break where the other column intervenes. Every quote in all four of my files was run through common/tools/quotecheck.py: 25 card quotes, 4 claim-update quotes (the fifth is deliberately empty) and 11 Notion-finding quotes all pass, 0 not found. (b) The one claim-update entry with an empty quote is the C081 extra-study entry for Christoph 1988: its deciding sentence is from Christoph's abstract, and quotecheck validates the quote field against texts/S-686-35.txt whenever paper_id is set, so an abstract quote there would be dropped. The verbatim abstract sentences are in S-686-35_extra_studies.json under quote_from_abstract, which the checker does not read, and the brief's writing rule 4 allows the empty quote with a design description in its place. (c) Amass unavailable as stated above. (d) No content filter stopped any write; every file was written. (e) No paywall, login or bot check was encountered: the paper text was already extracted, and all lookups were Europe PMC metadata.
